Model verification for Edinburgh: forecasts made 1/3/5/7 days ahead vs ERA5 reanalysis, last 40 days (temp_mae in °C, lower is better; wet_dry_hit_pct = share of days the model got right whether it would rain over 1 mm). 'Claude (this page)' is your own previous forecasts, scored the same way (its rain call counts a chance of 50% or more, or medium or high risk, as rain); use its biases to correct yourself. 'reliability' scores your own rain chances (Brier, 0 is perfect) against ECMWF ENS on the same days and against the window's wet-day share, and your weekly tilts for the extended-range weeks against ERA5's weekly mean. 'station' is the same check against EGPH's own observed daily highs and lows (METAR; complete the next day, so it includes the last week that ERA5 hasn't reached; half-hourly integer readings, so its highs run a few tenths low). station.tmin_by_night is the airport-trained correction of the models' lows by type of night (per lead: each model's all-night bias, and per class the nights, the mean model bias on such a night (bias) and the part the blend removes after shrinkage (used_bias)); recent_1day the last nights one day ahead; blend_by_night the blend's own logged lows scored at the airport by the type of night it forecast, out of sample

tmin_by_night.rule: type of night from the models' mean hourly total cloud and 10 m wind, 18:00-08:00 local: clear and calm = wind under 10 km/h and cloud under 30%; calm, broken cloud = wind under 10 km/h and cloud under 75%; otherwise cloudy or windy. Each model's all-night bias at the airport, plus the class's extra bias shrunk by n/(n+5) for n nights; ERA5 bias, unsplit, where a model has under 14 airport nights at a lead

items.title: ECMWF seasonal ensemble by month for Edinburgh vs ERA5 1991-2020 normals. This is Open-Meteo's default seasonal series: EC46 (run daily) for about the first 46 days, then SEAS5 (started on the 1st of each month), 51 members joined by member number, on a 36 km grid, so the first month or two are mostly EC46. Raw model output, not bias-corrected: the model's own climate at this point differs from ERA5's normal by month and lead (the SEAS5 winter call's model_climate.by_month gives bias_c, and pct_members_warmer_than_model_climate for SEAS5 alone against its own climate), so pct_members_warmer_than_normal here mixes the forecast with that bias. Compare the spread and the shares, not the absolute values

ECMWF's own implied calls on the cold-winter event, from the point members. pct_members_colder_than_normal (logged beside your call and scored as the rival 'ECMWF SEAS5') is the share of the 51 members of the default series above (EC46 for about 46 days, then SEAS5, joined by member number, so its December is mostly EC46) with a December-February mean of (daily max + min) / 2 below the ERA5 1991-2020 normal. It is raw model output, so it mixes the forecast with the model's own error at this point, and it is against ERA5, not the ERA5-Land the odds are scored on. pct_members_colder_than_model_climate is SEAS5 alone (model_climate.run_start is the first month of the reply; in the first days of a month the newest run can still be the month before): the share of its members whose December-February mean is below SEAS5's own climate for the same start month and lead (ECMWF's monthly anomaly, from its re-forecasts; model_climate.climate says which years). That removes the model's mean error at this point (model_climate.by_month gives it month by month as bias_c, the model climate minus the ERA5 normal) but not errors in the spread, and it is not calibrated on the model's past skill. model_climate.djf.pct_range_for_rounding is how far the 0.1 °C rounding of ECMWF's figures can move it; pct_same_members_colder_than_era5_normal is the same SEAS5 members against the ERA5 normal without the correction, so the three shares separate the EC46 part from the bias part. None of them is the answer: they are inputs to weigh

model_climate.note: The model climate is the mean of the past forecasts that SEAS5 makes for the same start month and the same lead. A share below this climate removes the mean error of the model at this point. It does not correct the spread of the members, the change in climate between the two periods, or the difference between ERA5 and ERA5-Land.

items.title: Polar vortex strength: zonal-mean zonal wind at 60°N (m/s, daily UTC mean, positive = westerly) at 10 hPa (the standard SSW level: a reversal to easterly is a major sudden stratospheric warming) and 50 hPa (lower stratosphere), per model; ensembles give mean/p10/p90/min across members and the % of members easterly. Early-warning signs from the single runs: polar_cap_t10 = area-mean temperature over 60-90°N at 10 hPa (°C; a jump of 20 °C or more in a few days is a sudden warming under way), heat_flux_100 = eddy heat flux v'T' around 60°N at 100 hPa (K m/s; sustained high values push wave energy up and tend to weaken the vortex 1-2 weeks later; w1 and w2 are the parts of it carried by zonal wavenumbers 1 and 2: a pulse mostly in wave 1 tends to displace the vortex, one with a large wave-2 part to stretch and split it), waves_10hPa = amplitude in metres of zonal wavenumber 1 and 2 in the 10 hPa geopotential height around 60°N (wave 1 growing to well over 1000 m means the vortex is being displaced off the pole; wave 2 growing to several hundred metres means it is being stretched towards a split; in winter a few hundred metres each is ordinary; waves_vs_season places today against this season's analysed days). wave2_by_level gives, per single run and day, the longitude (°E, 0-180; the second ridge is 180° further east) of the wave-2 ridges in the 60°N height at 500, 100 and 10 hPa, their amplitudes, and the tilt (10 hPa ridge minus 500 hPa ridge): a ridge that shifts west with height (negative tilt, e.g. 45°E at 500, 29°E at 100, 6°E at 10 hPa) with ridges near the Urals and Alaska is the structure of a split. For ensembles, pct_members_ever_easterly is the share of members that reverse on any day of the run (the SSW probability for that window; the per-day share understates it) and reversal_median_date the typical timing. Days before 2026-11-16 are analysis.

items.title: Arctic Oscillation (AO), North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) and Pacific-North American pattern (PNA) indices, NOAA CPC's standardised daily values (AO from 1000 hPa height, NAO and PNA from 500 hPa): last 10 days observed and CPC's GEFS forecast (31 members: mean/p10/p90/min/max, % negative). An index whose file failed this run is left out. Negative AO/NAO favours blocking and cold spells in the UK; positive, mild westerlies. A positive PNA goes with a deep Aleutian low, the pattern El Niño favours, which adds to the wave 1 that goes up into the stratosphere; a negative PNA during an El Niño means the atmosphere is not following it.

Slow climate drivers: QBO (monthly equatorial zonal wind at 30 and 50 hPa, m/s; easterly QBO makes a weak vortex and SSWs more likely), ENSO (weekly Niño 3.4 SST anomaly and the ONI and the Relative ONI, RONI, which takes the tropical mean warming out, °C; La Niña below -0.5, El Niño above +0.5; the El Niño tables call +1.0 to +1.5 strong and +1.5 or more very strong) and the MJO (last 10 days, Wheeler-Hendon phase 1-8 and amplitude; amplitude under 1 means weak). MJO phases 6-7 tend to favour a negative NAO 1-2 weeks later. More ENSO keys, each missing when its source failed (anomalies in °C against 1991-2020): regions_weekly, the last 8 weeks of CPC's four weekly Niño regions (1+2, 3, 3.4, 4) with e_index and c_index, the east and central Pacific indices; region_records, each region's latest week ranked among every week since September 1981 (rank 1 = the warmest, 'of' = weeks in the record), with the highest of the last 52 weeks and the previous record, the highest week before those 52; flavour, a word from E and C over the last 4 weeks by the rule given with it; same_weeks, those 4 weeks this year and the same weeks of the earlier years with the highest mean Niño 3.4 there (years_compared = years the record covers), each with its four regions, E, C and flavour, to show which past event this one is like; mei, PSL's Multivariate ENSO Index v2 (standardised, no unit: sea level pressure, SST, surface winds and outgoing longwave radiation over the tropical Pacific, so it measures the atmosphere's part too), the last 6 two-month seasons, and the latest ranked among the same season of every year since 1979, with previous_record the highest of the other years; relative_nino34, NOAA OISST v2.1 against PSL's 1991-2020 daily mean: the Niño 3.4 box (5°S-5°N, 170-120°W) anomaly minus the 20°S-20°N mean anomaly (sea cells every 1° of latitude and 2° of longitude; 'cells' = how many), as the mean of the last 'days' days (7, fewer in early January) and the latest day. relative_nino34 is NOT the RONI and will not match it: CPC's RONI also multiplies the difference by a variance factor, is a 3-month mean and comes from ERSST, while this is unscaled, about a week, and from OISST.

flavour.rule: E = Niño 1+2 - 0.5 x Niño 4 and C = 1.7 x Niño 4 - 0.1 x Niño 1+2 (the published approximation of Takahashi et al. 2011, from the weekly anomalies, °C). The larger of |E| and |C| says warm or cold; then east Pacific when E is more than twice C, central Pacific when C is more than twice E (both with the sign of a cold event turned over), mixed between; no word when neither reaches 0.5

Polar-cap geopotential height: the cos-weighted 60-90°N mean at 10, 50, 100 and 500 hPa as a standardised anomaly (sd) against an NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 daily climatology for 1991-2020, its linear trend carried forward to the date, per model and day. Positive = a cap higher than normal, i.e. a weak or displaced vortex; +1 sd at 100 hPa is the usual threshold for a stratospheric anomaly that couples to the surface (a negative AO/NAO in the following weeks), and +2 to +3 sd at 10 hPa is a major disturbance. ECMWF HRES runs from 45 days back (its past runs), the other single runs from yesterday; ensembles give the mean, 10th and 90th percentiles and the share of members at +1 sd or more each day, and the share reaching +1 sd on any day of the run. ECMWF ENS also at 500 hPa: its share of members at +1 sd there by day says when the event reaches the troposphere. headline: each model's value today and its forecast peak (ECMWF ENS: also the 500 hPa share by day and the first day half the members reach +1 sd). gfs_section: the same from the 1° GFS on 17 levels from 1000 to 10 hPa (the dripping-paint chart as numbers)

periods.text: A changeable pattern is likely during this period with Atlantic frontal systems spreading across the UK. This means spells of rain and perhaps strong winds will move over the UK at times, with cooler, drier interludes between systems. Rainfall will probably be most frequent in parts of the south and west and some snow is likely in the north at times. Temperatures are expected to be near normal overall, mildest in the south and coldest in the north.

The tracks of low pressure systems will likely track farther farther south than normal during this period. This means that rainfall will probably be focussed across the south of the UK; conversely, higher pressure to the north means drier conditions here. Temperatures in the south will probably be near normal or perhaps slightly above at times, with the north colder than normal.

The widespread warmth across the Northern Hemisphere (NH) this past summer and now the fall has continued into November (see Figure). However, high-latitude blocking in the North Atlantic sector has resulted in colder temperatures in Europe and especially Siberia and into Northeast Asia (see Figure). Troughing in the Gulf of Alaska has resulted in very mild temperatures for North America (see Figure). However, the very large PV disruption ongoing, in my opinion will resolve into a stretched PV. Stretched PVs first result in cold temperatures in East Asia followed by a colder pattern in North America. So despite the indefinite reign of mild weather across North America predicted by the weather models, I expect colder temperatures to arrive ashore across North America late November and/or early December. And as I am fond of saying one good (PV) stretch deserves another. Figure. While the rest of the meteorological community has been focused on the super El Niño, my focus this fall has been stretched polar vortex (PV) events. Back in late September (28 Sep 2026) I noted a very early stretched PV and posed two questions to ponder. Could this be a foreshadowing by the atmosphere for the winter? Since 2013 the canonical sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) extended Greenland blocking pathway is no longer in operation, instead we seem to be in a paradigm where all PV disruptions of the cold kind are PV stretching (obviously an exaggeration but to first order true). Since then, I have been arguing with myself saying based on the SSW the best analog for November 2026 is November 2009. However, 2009 is clearly in the “before times,” and now there is a new Sherrif in town, or of you prefer a new paradigm in operation. In 2009 the SSW-negative NAO ruled and today we are under new management and the PV stretch-negative North Pacific Oscillation rules. And when the models first caught on to the possibility of an SSW and excitement was building for the expected tropospheric response of a long duration Greenland block/negative NAO, I shared with USA Today don’t be surprised if this all resolves as yet just another stretched PV (USA Today 26Oct2026). Arctic Sea Ice I am and will continue to watch Arctic sea ice. Current conditions are shown in Figure 16. It has been shown that less sea ice in the North Atlantic sector of the Arctic weakens the polar vortex while less sea ice in the North Pacific sector strengthens the polar vortex. Sea ice has been growing a decent clip, but clearly more in the North Pacific sector than the North Atlantic sector and therefore Arctic sea ice anomalies continue to show a strong focus or weighting of negative anomalies towards the North Atlantic sector relative to the North Pacific sector and this is a robust signal of an overall weaker PV this winter. In fact with sea ice near normal in the North Pacific sector and well below normal in the North Atlantic sector looks nearly optimal for perturbing the PV. I believe that the lack of sea ice in the Barents-Kara Seas may have contributed to the record strong high-pressure Ural/Scandinavian blocking and the unprecedentedly early weak PV that so far resembles more of an SSW than the more common stretched PV this time of year. items.title: Analog winters for Edinburgh: the 5 past winters (since 1979/80) most like this autumn in vortex strength (mean 60°N 10 hPa wind over the last 30 days, m/s), ENSO (RONI (Niño 3.4 less the tropical mean), °C; now.distance_index says which, and oni is given beside it) and QBO (30 hPa wind, m/s), each in standard deviations of the record, with equal weight, closest first; for each, its major SSW date if any and Edinburgh's Dec/Jan/Feb mean temperature anomaly vs 1991-2020 (°C, ERA5) with snow and frost days. Five analogs are a small sample: treat them as a tilt in the odds, and compare with all_winters. chance_check says whether they say more than 10000 random sets of as many winters would (trend removed): within chance, they shouldn't move the odds. early_ssw_winters is every winter in the record with a major SSW by 31 December, the reference class when an early warming is under way or forecast, with the same check. enso_qbo_winters is a second reference set, the five nearest on ENSO and the QBO only, with its own chance_check: the vortex term can keep out a winter that matches on El Niño and the QBO. method_skill is how this method has done on the record: each past winter in turn matched against the others by today's rule and calendar window (leave one out), for the variables in use (in_use) and without the vortex term (without_vortex); djf_correlation is between the analogs' mean detrended Dec-Feb and the winter's own, against r_critical_5pct, the value chance reaches or passes about one time in 20 with as many winters (one-sided and approximate; a negative correlation is no result either way); djf_sign_right counts the winters whose sign (milder or colder than the trend) the analogs got right, against djf_sign_right_by_chance; ssw_brier scores the analogs' SSW share as a chance of a major SSW (0 is perfect) against ssw_base_rate_brier, always calling the other winters' rate. When verdict is no measurable skill, the analogs carry no information the record does not, and must not move the odds. novelty: today's distance to its nearest analog (nearest_now) against every past winter's distance to its own nearest (median, 90th percentile, largest), today's z-score on each variable, beyond_record for any variable outside the record's range, and outside_record when today is farther from its nearest analog than any past winter was: then no past winter is a true analog

Major sudden stratospheric warmings by the month they start, for the ssw_*_pct calls: the definition the calls are scored on, how often each month from November to February has had one since 1979/80 (reference_pct is the rate the calls are scored against), this season so far (NASA's analysis and GEOS-FP's 10-day forecast), and how dated calls made before each month began have scored (Brier, 0 is perfect): yours, and other people's public calls, which are here to be scored, not as evidence. el_nino_model, when present, scales the reference rates for this El Niño with an idealised model (rate_ratio is a range; its text, hindcast and live scores say how far to trust it; its input is the ONI, as the plan fixes, and sensitivity.roni, when present, gives the same figures with the RONI as the input, a sensitivity figure that is never logged or scored). after_ssw: how often another major SSW started within 30, 60 and 90 days of one, in the record since 1979 (all, and those by 31 December) and in the model. by_enso_qbo: how many winters since 1979/80 had a major SSW under the same definition (any: November to March; dec_feb; jan_feb) by El Niño class on the August-October ONI and on the RONI (very strong +1.5 or more, strong +1.0 to +1.5, weak to moderate +0.5 to +1.0, neutral, La Niña -0.5 or less; winters named with their SSW start dates when 8 or fewer), by the QBO's phase in October at 30 and at 50 hPa (west: wind 0 or more), and for this winter's cell (this_year: its class on the index the analogs use, and its QBO phase at 30 hPa), with each winter in the cell named. Each count comes with the share of all possible sets of as many winters from the record with as many or as few (random_sets_with_as_many_pct, random_sets_with_as_few_pct). A verdict of too few winters to tell means the group is so small that no count at all could fall outside chance (0 of 3 winters is one): it is not evidence of no difference, and it is not evidence of a difference. Within chance means a larger group that is no different from any winters. cells gives how many checks the table holds, how many fell outside chance, how many chance alone gives (expected_outside_by_chance, exact) and how many are too_few_to_tell. The groups at +1.0 or more hold a few winters each, so read them as counts. this_season.earliest_in_record: the earliest start in a season (from 1 July) of a major SSW in this record before this season, and whether this season's first one is earlier (this_is_earliest); call an event record-early only from this, and say the record is NASA MERRA-2 since its from_season

data.definition: a major sudden stratospheric warming starts in that month. On a day in the month, the zonal-mean wind at 60°N, 10 hPa (NASA MERRA-2, and GEOS-FP for this season) turns easterly. This occurs at least 20 westerly days after any earlier event. Before 30 April, the wind is westerly again for 10 days in a row (Charlton and Polvani). A reversal with no recovery is the final warming, and it does not count

Central England, not the location; pre-1979 'SSW' winters are inferred, not measured. enso_classes (null if Niño 3.4 could not be fetched): every winter since 1870/71 by El Niño class on the August-October mean of Niño 3.4 (HadISST) against its own era, classes fixed in advance (very strong +1.5 or more, strong +1.0 to +1.5, weak to moderate +0.5 to +1.0, neutral, La Niña -0.5 or less). Per class: the number of winters and, for November, December, January, February, March, December-February and late_minus_early (January-February minus November-December, so negative means the late winter was colder than the early winter), the mean in °C against each winter's own era (a 31-year mean, which takes out the long-term warming), colder (how many winters were below their era; for late_minus_early, how many had the colder late winter), and where the mean falls among 10,000 random sets of as many winters (random_5_95, random_sets_below_pct, verdict; within chance means any winters picked at random do as well). top_class_winters lists the very strong winters month by month. cells says how many class-by-month means were checked, how many fell outside chance and how many chance alone gives (about one in ten): one extreme cell among many is not proof. For the last 15 winters the 31-year window has only earlier years in it, so its mean is moved along the 61-year trend of the November-March mean (2015/16 and 2023/24, two of the very strong winters, are in that zone, and the move takes about 0.1 to 0.2 °C off them); Niño 3.4 for those years is against the earlier years only. this_year is this winter's class from CPC's ONI (RONI beside it), as the Niño 3.4 file lags. ECMWF extended range (EC46, 51 members via Open-Meteo) to day 46, at the surface: the Arctic index is the cos-weighted 60-90°N mean sea-level pressure (positive = high pressure over the pole = a negative-AO pattern, the surface end of a stratospheric event coupling down), the NAO the Azores-minus-Iceland pressure (negative = blocked NAO-), both in sd against NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 for 1991-2020 after the model's own offset is taken off. days: ensemble mean, 10th/90th percentiles and the share of members at +1 sd or more (Arctic) or -1 or below (NAO) each day; weeks: Monday-Sunday means; headline: the peak, the low and the days past day 15; model_climate: the weekly ensemble-mean anomalies in hPa against ECMWF's re-forecast climate (all 100 members), which need no reanalysis. Extended-range skill for the AO and NAO is modest past week 3: read shifts in the mean and the share of members, not a single date

Winter base rates for Edinburgh (since 1950/51; ERA5-Land at the point for the cold winter and the cold spell, ERA5's 0.25° cell for the wet winter and the stormy winter): how often each of the four winter-outlook events happened, under the exact definitions the odds use, for 1991-2020, the last 15 winters and all of them; the lines the wet and stormy winters are judged against (djf_precip_normal_mm, storm_days_normal: the 1991-2020 means); the last 15 winters one by one (with djf_precip_vs_normal_pct and storm_days); this season so far (precipitation as a percentage of normal for the December-February days in, and the stormy days so far: the stormy winter has happened once storm_days_so_far is above storm_days_normal); and how your own past calls scored (Brier score, 0 is perfect, against always calling the 1991-2020 base rate; null until a winter is over). The ERA5 gust is for a whole grid cell, so a station's gust is often stronger. by_el_nino (null if neither index could be fetched): the same winters by El Niño class on the August-October value, once on CPC's ONI and once on the RONI (Niño 3.4 less the tropical mean, so a warmer ocean does not read as El Niño), classes fixed in advance (very strong +1.5 or more, strong +1.0 to +1.5, weak to moderate +0.5 to +1.0, neutral, La Niña -0.5 or less); this_year gives this winter's class on each. Per class: the winters (named when 8 or fewer); counts of cold_winter, cold_spell, wet_winter and stormy_winter under the exact definitions above, each with the share of all possible sets of as many winters from the record with as many or as few (verdict within chance means the class is no different from any winters; too few winters to tell means the class is so small that no count could fall outside chance, which is not evidence either way); and the December-February, December, January and February means in °C with the record's linear warming trend taken out (trend_c_per_decade), with how many were colder than the trend and where each mean falls among 10,000 random sets of as many winters. strongest lists every winter at +1.0 or more one by one. since_1990_at_1_0_or_more is the same for the winters since 1990/91 at +1.0 or more, checked against the other winters since 1990/91 only: the fixed 1991-2020 cold-winter line is easier to miss now that winters are milder. cells says how many checks a table holds, how many fell outside chance, how many chance alone gives (expected_outside_by_chance) and how many are too_few_to_tell. The classes at +1.0 or more hold only a handful of winters each, so read them as tilts, not as rules

analysis.summary: A yellow Met Office ice warning covers Lothian and Borders until 10:00 today. The airport fell to -3 °C overnight and had 0 °C under a clear sky at 08:50 UTC. A front brings 10-16 mm of rain and gusts near 50 km/h on Tuesday, with wet snow only on the Pentlands tops at first. Showery rain on Wednesday gives way to a cold northerly, then hard frosts on 20-21 November. Atlantic fronts return from late on 21 November, and the week to 1 December stays changeable and near normal.

days.summary:
Observed: the airport fell to -2 °C at 07:20 UTC, and its 24-hour minimum was -3 °C. At 08:50 UTC it had 0 °C, a west wind of 13 km/h, a clear sky and 1004 hPa.

The Met Office yellow ice warning ends at 10:00. Untreated paths stay icy until the sun warms them near midday.

The day is dry and sunny. Chance above 1 mm: 0% in ECMWF ENS, AIFS ENS, GEM ENS, UKMO ENS and ICON-EPS, 16% in GEFS and 19% in AIGEFS. I set 3%.

Highs: hourly guidance 4.2 °C at 14:00, blend 4.7 °C, ECMWF ENS 4.0 °C and UKMO ENS 5.7 °C. My highs ran 0.4 °C cold one day ahead, so I set 4.5 °C.

The wind increases after 01:00, with gusts of 34-38 km/h from 02:00. Rain arrives near 06:00. The hourly guidance makes it heaviest at 07:00-11:00, at 1.0-1.2 mm an hour.

Snow falls in 77% of GEFS members and 73% of AIFS ENS members, but in 0% of ECMWF ENS. ECMWF ENS gives lying snow in 0% of members. The freezing level rises to 970 m by 14:00, so the hills turn to rain too.

medium_range.summary:
I weight the ensembles over the single runs from day 5. Confidence is low from 22 November.

Single runs, 23-26 November:
- ECMWF HRES puts a 994 hPa low west of Ireland on 23 November, with a southerly over Scotland.
- On 26 November ECMWF HRES builds a 1027-1028 hPa high north of Scotland and puts a 1003 hPa low over Cornwall. That gives Edinburgh a fresh easterly.
- JMA has a 1025 hPa high north of Scotland on 23 November and a 1035 hPa high over Denmark on 26 November. It is the most blocked run.
- NAVGEM puts a 1005 hPa low over south-east England on 23 November, so Edinburgh gets a north-easterly.
- AIFS (machine learning) and GEM keep a 986-990 hPa low west of Ireland on 26 November, with a southerly. AIFS has -1 to 0 °C at 850 hPa over Scotland.
- GFS has about -4 °C at 850 hPa over Scotland on 23 November, and 0 °C on 25 November.

Ensemble means:
- The ECMWF ENS mean on 26 November has a 995 hPa low south of Greenland, 1000-1005 hPa west of the UK and 1015 hPa over Scandinavia. That gives a southerly to south-westerly.
- The AIFS ENS mean is similar, with a 990 hPa low south-west of Iceland. Its spread is 12-18 hPa there and over Norway.
- On 1 December the GEFS mean has a 1005 hPa low west of Ireland and 1015-1020 hPa over Greenland. The AIFS ENS mean has a 1000 hPa low south of Iceland, and its spread is 18-25 hPa over Scandinavia.

Temperatures and rain, 23-30 November:
- Mean highs: ECMWF ENS 6.7-8.3 °C (to 27 November), AIFS ENS 8.1-8.8 °C, GEM ENS 7.8-9.2 °C, AIGEFS 6.8-7.7 °C and GEFS 6.2-7.5 °C.
- Chance above 1 mm: ECMWF ENS 67-75%, GEFS 45-81%, AIFS ENS 37-67%, GEM ENS 43-67% and AIGEFS 45-65%.
- The GEFS 850 hPa mean is -2.5 to +0.9 °C, with a 10th percentile of -2 to -6.7 °C. The AIFS ENS mean is about 0 to +1.6 °C.

What ties it together: the stratospheric event of 10-12 November now reaches the troposphere. ECMWF ENS first has half its members at +1 sd at the 500 hPa polar cap on 25 November. But the Atlantic jet stays active, and most runs keep its lows west of Ireland. So Edinburgh sits between a Scandinavian high and Atlantic lows, in a southerly with rain at times.

This is again a block that forms too far east for cold here. The air upwind is only moderately cold, and the seas round the UK are warmer than normal.

What can make this wrong: the high builds north of Scotland, as in ECMWF HRES and JMA on 26 November. The low is then to the south. Then Edinburgh gets an easterly with -4 to -6 °C at 850 hPa, North Sea showers, sleet in the city and snow on the hills. Snow to sea level needs air near -8 °C, and only 4-12% of ECMWF members show that over Copenhagen on 23-28 November.
signals: Frost and ice: the blend gives the airport -2.3 °C (frost 78%) on 20 November and -2.7 °C (81%) on 21 November. ECMWF ENS gives ice in 55% of members on 21 November, when rain reaches frozen ground.
Rain: ensemble means are 9.5-19.4 mm on 17 November and 4.0-7.3 mm on 18 November. The ECMWF ENS 90th percentile on 17 November is 21.8 mm.

AO and NAO (NOAA CPC): the observed AO is +0.06 and the NAO -1.00 on 15 November. GEFS takes the AO to +1.08 on 20 November, then to -1.80 on 30 November, with 84% of members negative. The NAO stays near 0 to 28 November, then -0.48 on 30 November (74% negative).
PNA: +1.55 observed on 15 November. GEFS keeps it at +0.34 to +1.19, with at most 3% of members negative. The atmosphere follows El Niño, and the deep Aleutian low adds to the upward wave 1.

ECMWF regimes (15 November): NAO- at 76-100% on 17-19 November and the Atlantic Ridge at about 50-85% on 20-21 November. NAO+ then leads from 22 November to 2 December at 37-49%, with Blocking at 7-30%.
EPO: ECMWF ENS reaches -1.15 on 21 November, with 61% of members at -1 or below. GEFS has 29% and AIFS ENS 14% at -1 or below on that day.

Pacific chain: the East Asian mountain torque reached +4.03 sd on 8 November. AAM rose to +2.92 sd on 14 November and is +2.82 sd on 15 November, with a 7-day change of +2.15. The GWO is in phase 6 at amplitude 2.95 on 13 November, the El Niño-like state. The EPO turns negative on 18-25 November and the heat flux pulses on 21 November, so the chain follows. AAM did not start to fall, so it gives no ridge signal yet, and the GFS has no new torque event to 23 November.

Heat flux (100 hPa, 60°N ring) on 21 November: ECMWF HRES 38.5, AIFS 36.6, UKMO 33.9, GEM 30.2 and GFS 29.4 K m/s. Wave 2 carries more than wave 1 on that day. The severe-weather.eu ensemble means (100 hPa, 45-75°N) peak near 22-23 K m/s on 22 November, under their 90th percentile of 26.6 K m/s.

Upwind cold (ECMWF ENS, 850 hPa at -8 °C or below, 23-28 November): Oslo 22-31%, Stockholm 22-29%, Helsinki 29-39% and Copenhagen only 4-12%. Moscow has 49-73%, but it lies south-east of the usual track. Snow lies in 61-76% of members at Oslo but in 0-6% at Stockholm, Helsinki and Copenhagen.
Snow cover (Rutgers): Eurasia has 14.55 million km², below the normal of 16.06 million km² and rank 41 of 61. The October gain in Eurasia was near normal, rank 29.

Sea temperatures: the CDAS map (Tropical Tidbits, against 1981-2010) shows the seas round the UK about +0.4 to +1.6 °C. It also shows a cold patch near 45-55°N, 30-50°W with warm subtropics, a positive-NAO pattern. Coral Reef Watch (against 1985-2012) shows warm open water in the Barents and Kara Seas.

MJO: the analysed OMI is phase 4 at amplitude 1.31 on 11 November. ECMWF ENS reaches phase 4 near 1.5 by day 5, then goes inside the circle in phases 1-3 by days 15-20. The bias-corrected GEFS is near or inside the circle in phases 3-4 to 29 November. Neither reaches phases 6-7.

model_agreement.summary:
To 18 November the models agree well. Every run has a cold, dry day today, rain on Tuesday and showery rain on Wednesday. They differ on the Tuesday amount, 6.8 mm (UKMO) to 19.6 mm (GFS), and on the gusts, 42.5-65.5 km/h.

On 19-21 November they agree on a cold northerly, then a ridge with hard frost. They differ on when the next front arrives on 21 November. GFS and GEM keep the cold air all day, but ICON and AIFS bring 9.5-10.2 °C.

From 23 November the runs split. ECMWF HRES and JMA build a high north of Scotland or over Denmark by 26 November, which gives an easterly. AIFS (machine learning), GEM and the ensemble means keep an Atlantic low west of Ireland and a southerly.

On the 40-day scorecard against ERA5, ICON is best one day ahead (0.6 °C), then the blend (0.7 °C), and AIFS and my own forecasts (0.9 °C). ECMWF HRES, ARPEGE and AIGFS run 1.3 °C cold on highs one day ahead. At the airport every model runs warm on lows one day ahead, by 0.5 °C (GEM) to 2.7 °C (GFS).

My lows ran 1.2-1.4 °C warm at the airport, and my highs 0.4-0.9 °C cold against ERA5. This morning I ran warm again: I set -1.5 °C, and the airport reached -3 °C. ICON-EPS and GEM ENS gave frost in only 0-2% of members for this morning.

models.view: 16.1 mm and gusts of 55 km/h on 17 November, 4.8 mm on 18 November. Dry on 20-23 November, with lows of -0.9 °C and 0.8 °C on 20-21 November. A 994 hPa low west of Ireland on 23 November. On 26 November a 1028 hPa high north of Scotland and a 1003 hPa low over Cornwall, so a fresh easterly. Its highs run 1.3 °C cold on the scorecard.

100% above 1 mm on 17 November (mean 14.9 mm, 90th percentile 21.8 mm) and 94% on 18 November. Frost in 84% of members on 20 November and 67% on 21 November, with ice in 55% on 21 November. The mean on 26 November has a 995 hPa low south of Greenland and a southerly over the UK. Rain in 67-75% of members on 22-27 November.

AIFS has 14.8 mm on 17 November, 10.2 °C on 21 November and 9.1 mm on 22 November, the mildest run. It keeps a deep low west of Ireland on 26 November, with -1 to 0 °C at 850 hPa over Scotland. AIFS ENS gives 100% above 1 mm on 17-18 November and snow in 73% of members on 17 November.

GFS has 19.6 mm and gusts of 66 km/h on 17 November, and 9.0 mm on 18 November. It keeps 21 November cold at 3.5 °C, with 7.7 mm late. It has about -4 °C at 850 hPa over Scotland on 23 November. GEFS is the coldest ensemble, with an 850 hPa mean of -5.4 °C on 20 November and snow in 77% of members on 17 November.

AIGFS has 13.9 mm on 17 November and is dry on 20-25 November. AIGEFS is the wettest ensemble on 17 November, with a mean of 19.4 mm and 100% above 1 mm. It gives frost in only 32% of members on 20 November and 3% on 21 November.

ICON has the best one-day score (0.6 °C) and the top weight in the blend to 18 November. It has 10.1 mm on 17 November and 10.9 mm on 18 November, and 9.5-10.0 °C on 21-22 November. ICON-EPS gave frost in 2% of members for this morning, but the airport reached -3 °C.

UKMO has 6.8 mm on 17 November and 8.0 mm on 18 November. It has a clear night and -2.2 °C on 21 November, then 4.6 mm on 22 November. Its 850 hPa map has -2 to -4 °C over Scotland on 21 November. UKMO ENS gives frost in 89% of members on 21 November.

GEM has 11.3 mm and gusts of 64 km/h on 17 November. It keeps 21-23 November cold and dry, then a 986 hPa low west of Ireland on 26 November and gusts of 59 km/h on 24 November. GEM ENS is the mildest ensemble after 22 November, with mean highs of 7.8-9.2 °C and 0% frost.

ARPEGE has 7.4 mm and gusts of 59 km/h on 17 November, and only 1.9 mm on 18 November. JMA has a 1025 hPa high north of Scotland on 23 November and a 1035 hPa high over Denmark on 26 November, the most blocked run. NAVGEM has a 1005 hPa low over south-east England on 23 November.

extended_range.summary:
The ECMWF weekly maps, regimes, meteogram, Hovmöller, MJO and 46-day wind charts are from the 15 November run. The EC46 surface indices are from the 16 November run, and Simon Lee's index is from the 14 November run.

Edinburgh weekly meteogram (medians as I read them):
- 2 m temperature: about -1.5 °C for the week to 23 November, about +1.0 °C to 30 November and +1.2 °C to 7 December.
- After that: about +0.7 °C to 14 December, near 0 °C to 21 December and about -0.3 °C to 28 December.
- Precipitation: about 10 mm above normal for the week to 23 November and about 5 mm above to 30 November, then near normal.
- Pressure: well below the model climate in the week to 23 November, then near normal with a wide spread.

Weekly maps:
- 23-30 November: MSLP is 10-20 hPa below normal west of Ireland and 5-10 hPa above over Scandinavia. 500 hPa heights are high over the North Sea and Scandinavia. Scotland is 0 to +1 °C and England +1 to +3 °C.
- 30 November to 7 December: Scotland 0 to +1 °C, and England and France +1 to +3 °C.
- 7-14 December: weak high pressure over Greenland and Finland, near normal over the UK. Heights are high from Iberia to Scandinavia, and the UK is 0 to +1 °C.
- 21-28 December: weak high pressure over Greenland and lower pressure over the south-west Atlantic. The UK is 0 to +1 °C.

EC46 500 hPa over the North Pole: heights stay low over Siberia and the North Pacific side in all four weeks. They are high over Greenland and the Canadian Arctic from 30 November. In the week from 23 November a low lobe reaches from Greenland towards the UK. So the AO signal in the mean is mixed.

EC46 surface indices (51 members, 16 November):
- Arctic index: -0.98 sd in the week from 16 November, then -0.09, +0.07, -0.13, -0.21 and -0.18 sd. The peak is +0.14 sd on 30 November, with 14% of members above +1 sd.
- NAO: +0.17 sd in the week from 23 November, then -0.07 to +0.01 sd. Against the model climate it is +8.5 hPa that week, then -2.3 to -4.6 hPa from 7 December.
- Skill for the AO and NAO is modest past week 3, so I read the shares, not single dates.

Hovmöller (35-60°N), as I read it:
- At 0° a trough sits near the UK on about 16-20 November, then a ridge on about 21-25 November.
- At 25-50°E a trough sits on about 20-25 November. With the ridge at 0°, that gives a northerly window over the North Sea for about 3 days, near 21-24 November. Edinburgh sits under the ridge, so it gets frost, not a northerly.
- After 26 November the anomalies are weak, 2-4 dam against a spread of 6-12 dam. A trough near 25°W shows on about 27 November to 2 December.

MJO: ECMWF ENS reaches phase 4 near 1.5 by day 5 and is inside the circle by days 15-20. The bias-corrected GEFS is near or inside the circle in phases 3-4. Neither reaches phases 6-7, so the MJO gives no push to a negative NAO.

Met Office (20 November to 14 December): changeable to 29 November, with Atlantic fronts, rain, strong winds at times and some snow in the north. Then lows track further south, the north is drier, and the north is colder than normal.
- I agree on a changeable spell to 29 November, near normal overall.
- I differ on a cold north in early December. The ECMWF weekly maps keep Scotland at 0 to +1 °C, and NAO+ leads the ECMWF regimes to 2 December.

AER (Judah Cohen, 9 November, 7 days old): the AO negative to neutral and a stretched vortex. I agree on the stretch and on a short positive AO, which GEFS has at +0.6 to +1.1 on 16-21 November. I differ on depth: the 10 hPa wind reversed, so this is a major SSW under the scored rule.

weeks.pattern: A trough near the UK with rain on 17-18 November, then a cold northerly and a ridge with hard frost on 20-21 November. The meteogram median is about -1.5 °C, with about 10 mm more rain than normal.

A Scandinavian high and a deep trough west of Ireland give a southerly with rain at times. NAO+ leads at 38-49%. ECMWF HRES and JMA show an easterly risk near 26 November. The meteogram median is about +1.0 °C.
NAO+ and Blocking are close, at 33-41% and 25-39%. The EC46 NAO is near 0. Scotland is 0 to +1 °C and England +1 to +3 °C. The meteogram median is about +1.2 °C.
Weak high pressure over Greenland and Finland, and heights high from Iberia to Scandinavia. Blocking and NAO+ are close at 24-39%. The UK is 0 to +1 °C.
NAO+ leads at 26-36%, with Blocking at 23-30%. The 10 hPa vortex is near 39-40 m/s in the 46-day chart, with a cold pole, which favours westerlies. The meteogram median is near 0 °C.
No regime clearly leads: NAO+ 24-33%, Blocking 17-32%, NAO- 12-19% and the Atlantic Ridge 9-19%. Weak high pressure over Greenland. The meteogram median is about -0.3 °C.

extended_range.regimes:
ECMWF regime probabilities (15 November run):
- NAO+ 100% on 15 November, NAO- 76-100% on 17-19 November and the Atlantic Ridge about 50-85% on 20-21 November.
- NAO+ then leads from 22 November to 2 December at 37-49%. Blocking grows from 7% on 23 November to 29-30% on 1-2 December.
- Blocking and NAO+ are close on 3-10 December, at 31-39% and 24-39%. Blocking leads on 4-5 and 8 December.
- From 11 December NAO+ leads again at 30-40%, with Blocking at 23-30%. NAO- and the Atlantic Ridge are each 6-19%.

Simon Lee's index (14 November run) uses a different scheme, so I compare only the time of the shifts. NAO+ peaks near +1.25 sd on 18 November and falls below 0 near 25 November. Scandinavian Blocking peaks near +0.65 sd on 24 November. NAO- rises to about +0.4 sd in early December and +0.7 sd on 16-18 December.

The two schemes agree on a shift near 21-24 November. They disagree on what comes after it. ECMWF's own regimes give NAO+ first, and Lee's index gives a Scandinavian block, then NAO- in December.

For Edinburgh, NAO+ brings mild, wet south-westerlies with fronts and gusts. A Scandinavian high with lows to the west gives a southerly or south-easterly, frost on clear nights and rain on fronts. North Sea showers in an easterly are rain or sleet near sea level. Snow at the coast needs air near -8 °C at 850 hPa.

stratosphere.summary:
Strength now:
- The 60°N wind at 10 hPa was easterly on 10-12 November. NASA GEOS had -2.9 m/s on 11 November and +2.0 m/s on 13 November, a record low for the date.
- On NASA MERRA-2 since 1979/80, this SSW (start 10 November) is the earliest in the record, before the event of 4 December 1981.
- Today the wind is westerly at 5.7-6.3 m/s in the single runs and 5.6 m/s in the ECMWF ENS mean (open_meteo, 60°N daily mean). GEFS has 5.1 m/s and GEPS 5.0 m/s. Severe-weather.eu and weatheriscool have 5.1 m/s (60°N, 00 UTC GFS analysis).
- NASA's climatology for 16 November has a record low of 6.8 m/s, a 10th percentile of 19.6 m/s and a mean of 30.1 m/s. So the vortex is still below the record low for the date.
- At 50 hPa the ECMWF ENS mean is 8.7 m/s. NASA GEOS had 7.5 m/s on 13 November, a record low for the date.
- The 10 hPa polar cap is -60.0 °C in ECMWF HRES. It cools to -68.4 °C by 22 November, near the NASA mean of -67.0 °C. No new warming is under way.

No new reversal in the forecast:
- ECMWF ENS to 28 November, AIFS ENS to 30 November, and GEFS and GEPS to 2 December give 0% of members easterly on any day. Severe-weather.eu gives 0% of 132 members to 1-2 December.
- The lowest members are 5.4 m/s (ECMWF ENS), 5.7 m/s (AIFS ENS), 4.8 m/s (GEFS) and 4.3 m/s (GEPS), all today.
- Severe-weather.eu says no SSW is expected in the next two weeks. That statement is about a new event, because a reversal already happened on 10-12 November.
- Under the scored rule a new event needs 20 westerly days after the last easterly day. NASA's first westerly day was 13 November, so the earliest start is about 2 December.

Recovery:
- Means on 28 November: ECMWF ENS 26.1 m/s, GEPS 31.5 m/s and GEFS 35.0 m/s. AIFS ENS has 33.4 m/s, with a bias of +2.7 m/s at 12-16 days, so about 31 m/s. The NASA mean for 28 November is 29.8 m/s.
- ECMWF HRES has 26.9 m/s on 28 November. GFS has 34.5 m/s, with a bias of +2.3 m/s at 12-16 days.
- AIFS (machine learning) has 22.9 m/s on 28 November, with a bias of +8.2 m/s at 12-16 days, so about 15 m/s. I give it little weight.
- The ECMWF 46-day chart (15 November) has a mean near 37 m/s on 3 December and near 39-40 m/s on 13-27 December. That is above its model-climate mean of 34-36 m/s.
- As I read that chart, one member reverses near 17-23 December and reaches about -12 m/s. Another reaches about -4 m/s on 31 December. That is 2 of about 100 lines, read from the chart, not a numeric share.
- The ECMWF weekly 10 hPa map for 14-21 December has a cold pole, 5-15 °C below the model climate. That is a strong vortex.

Early-warning signs:
- The October pulse was large: 46.4 K m/s on 29 October in the ECMWF HRES analysis (100 hPa, 60°N ring). Wave 2 carried most of it at first, then wave 1 took over in early November.
- The NASA 45-day mean (100 hPa, 45-75°N) is 12.4 K m/s, a record high for the date. The daily flux now is low: severe-weather.eu (100 hPa, 45-75°N) has 6.8 K m/s against a mean of 13.8 K m/s.
- A second pulse comes on 21 November (100 hPa, 60°N ring). ECMWF HRES has 38.5, AIFS 36.6, UKMO 33.9, GEM 30.2 and GFS 29.4 K m/s. Wave 2 carries 9.8-15.3 K m/s of it and wave 1 9.1-11.2 K m/s.
- The severe-weather.eu ensemble means (100 hPa, 45-75°N) peak near 22-23 K m/s on 22 November, under their 90th percentile of 26.6 K m/s. The single-run peaks above are for another band and were not compared with a percentile.
- The pulse meets a vortex that rebuilds, so no member reverses.

Shape: a displacement now, then a stretch, not a split.
- Wave 1 at 10 hPa is 772-781 m, at the 96th percentile of this season's 27 days. Wave 2 is 65-74 m, at the 4th percentile.

stratosphere.winter_impact:
The major SSW of 10-12 November is in the analysis. A new event cannot start before about 2 December, and no ensemble member reverses to 28 November - 2 December. After a major SSW, another started within 60 days in 2 of 31 cases since 1979. After an event by 31 December, this occurred in 0 of 4 cases.

The surface window starts when the 500 hPa polar cap turns positive in the ensembles. ECMWF ENS first has half its members at +1 sd on 25 November, so the window opens on about 24-28 November.

The surface answer is weaker than the cap suggests:
- EC46 (16 November) peaks its Arctic index at +0.14 sd on 30 November, with 14% of members above +1 sd.
- GEFS takes the AO to -1.80 on 30 November (84% negative), but the NAO only to -0.48 (74% negative).
- ECMWF makes NAO+ the most likely regime from 22 November to 2 December, at 37-49%.

For Edinburgh the high forms over Scandinavia, and the lows stay west of Ireland. That gives a southerly flow, near-normal temperatures, rain on fronts and frost on clear nights.

The cold risk is an easterly if the high builds north of Scotland, as ECMWF HRES shows on 26 November. The air upwind is only moderately cold. On 23-28 November, 22-31% of ECMWF members reach -8 °C at 850 hPa over Oslo and Stockholm, but only 4-12% over Copenhagen. Moscow is colder, at 49-73%, but it lies south-east of the usual track.

The seas round the UK are warm, so showers at the coast are rain or sleet, with snow on the Pentlands.

From early December the vortex rebuilds to about 37-40 m/s in the ECMWF 46-day run, with a cold pole in mid-December. A strong vortex favours mild, wet westerlies, so the cold risk falls in December.

winter_outlook.summary:
My call is a near-normal winter with a mild lean, and my confidence is low. The best cold chances come in a cold week to 22 November and a block from late November to mid-December. February holds a second, smaller easterly risk.

The odds are:
- December to February colder than the 1991-2020 normal: 30% (medium).
- A cold spell of 5 days or more from 1 November to 31 March: 48% (medium).
- December to February wetter than the 209 mm mean: 47%.
- More stormy days than the 17.6 mean: 44%.
- A major sudden stratospheric warming that starts in November: 100%. December 3%, January 18%, February 22%.

A major sudden stratospheric warming started on 10 November, and it couples down. More than half of the ECMWF members take the 500 hPa polar cap to +1 sd from 25 November. But the models put the high over Scandinavia and the low west of Ireland. That gives Edinburgh a south-easterly from a continent that is not cold, so temperatures stay near normal. The vortex then rebuilds fast, to about 38 m/s by mid-December.

The background points mild. A very strong El Nino, a westerly QBO, a warm North Sea and little snow upwind all work against cold that lasts. Seven of eight seasonal centres show a strongly negative NAO in February, with the low near the UK, so a late easterly risk stays open.
winter_outlook.basis:
I start from the 1991-2020 base rates, because the normals use that period. At Edinburgh, a cold December to February is 40%, a cold spell 43%, a wet winter 37% and a stormy winter 50%. The last 15 winters give 27%, 40%, 47% and 47%. The record warms by 0.24 °C a decade, so a mean below the fixed line is less common now. I begin the drivers near 31% for cold, 42% for a spell, 41% for wet and 48% for stormy.

The season data run to 10 November, with no spell days and no stormy days yet. My calls score only when the winter ends, so I have no bias to correct. My 13 cold-winter calls so far average 29%.

A major sudden stratospheric warming started on 10 November. NASA GEOS shows -2.9 m/s at 60°N and 10 hPa on 11 November, a record low for the date. The 10 hPa wind is westerly again near 5 m/s on 16 November, below the weakest value for the date in the ERA5 record, 7.7 m/s in 2009. This is the earliest major warming in the record, on NASA MERRA-2 since 1979/80. The earlier record start was 4 December 1981. All ECMWF and AIFS ensemble members turned easterly around 10 to 12 November.

The upper vortex recovers fast. The ECMWF ensemble mean reaches 24.3 m/s on 24 November and 26.1 m/s on 28 November, near the NASA 30th percentile. GEFS is faster, at 35.0 m/s on 28 November. No member of ECMWF ENS, AIFS ENS, GEFS or GEPS turns easterly again to 30 November. The EC46 chart takes the mean to about 38 m/s near mid-December, a little above its model climate. The scorecard shows AIFS too strong at 8 to 16 days, so I trust the physics ensembles for the rebuild.

The two depth measures disagree, so I give both. The 50 hPa wind stays westerly at 7 to 12 m/s, near the NASA 10th percentile. The 100 hPa polar cap reached +2.19 sd on 4 November. It returns above +1 sd on some day in 61% of ECMWF ENS members, 88% of AIFS ENS and 52% of GEPS. It returns in 0% of GEFS. Three of four ensembles show a clear share, so I call the event deep.

The 500 hPa cap sets the start of the surface window. ECMWF ENS takes 49% of members to +1 sd on 24 November and 59% on 26 November, with half from 25 November. In all, 75% of members reach +1 sd there on some day. Skill for the surface answer is modest past week 3, so I read the shares, not one run.

A negative AO is not the same as cold in Edinburgh. The ECMWF weekly maps for 23 to 30 November put +10 to +20 hPa over Scandinavia and a low west of Ireland. That gives a south-easterly from a continent that is not cold, and the UK runs 0 to +1 °C. The Edinburgh meteogram keeps that week near +0.5 °C and the December weeks at 0 to +0.5 °C. So the surface answer blocks the Atlantic, but it brings no deep cold here.

The week before is colder. The meteogram puts 16 to 22 November about 2 °C below normal, with most members below model climate. The Hovmoller shows a trough near 0 to 25°E on 16 to 19 November, then a ridge over the UK on 20 to 24 November. It shows no clear trough over eastern Europe with a ridge to the west to 15 December, so no long northerly window. The regime schemes disagree on 17 to 20 November, so I trust the meteogram, not the labels.

The ECMWF ENS mean 10 hPa maps put the vortex off the pole towards Scandinavia on 19 November. The vortex stretches from Canada to Siberia on 24 November and returns to the pole on 29 November. From 20 November the wave-2 ridges near the Urals and Alaska tilt west with height, by -49 to -67 degrees in ECMWF HRES. The 10 hPa wind rises at the same time, so I read a stretch, not a split. The hebweather centroid moves from 69°N back to about 82°N by day 15.

The first wave pulse peaked at 46.4 K m/s on 29 October, mostly in wave 2. A second pulse comes on 21 to 23 November in several runs. ECMWF HRES has 38.5 K m/s on 21 November, and GFS and AIFS reach 29.4 and 36.6 K m/s. It meets a vortex that rebuilds, so it stretches the vortex but reverses it in no member.

A cold surge pressed a high against the Tibetan Plateau on 8 November. The mountain torque over East Asia reached +4.0 sd that day. Global angular momentum rose from +0.3 sd on 7 November to +2.8 sd on 15 November. The Global Wind Oscillation sits in phase 6 at 2.95, the El Nino state with an extended Pacific jet. The PNA is +1.6, and ECMWF ENS puts 61% of members at an EPO of -1 or below on 21 November. GEFS puts 29% there, so the chain follows in part.

El Nino is very strong and east Pacific. The ONI is +2.46, the RONI +1.97 and the MEI v2 +2.53, rank 1 of 48. Nino 1+2 at +5.4 °C ranks 2nd and Nino 3 at +4.3 °C ranks 4th on record, with E at +4.76 against C at +1.71. The nearest same weeks are 1997 by flavour and 2015 by Nino 3.4. The PNA of +1.6 is a deep Aleutian low, so the atmosphere follows the ocean.

The class tables are one reference class in an older climate. On the RONI, Edinburgh had a cold December to February in 2 of 5 very strong winters, within chance. Since 1990, the 4 winters at +1.0 or more on the RONI were all milder, at +0.80 °C, milder than chance. Central England's 7 very strong winters averaged +1.20 °C against their era, with none colder. So I take a mild tilt, not a rule.

The seasonal maps are the November issue, with a nominal start of 1 November. So they do not include the warming that began on 10 November. In February, the C3S multi-system map, SEAS5, GloSea, CMCC, DWD, JMA and ECCC all put a strong Arctic high. Most put a low near or south of the UK. The SEAS5 NAO median is near -1.5 in January and -2.9 in February. For December to February as a whole the maps put the UK at 0 to +1 °C.

On balance the maps move the December to February cold odds up about 2 points. The mild mean pulls down, and the February NAO pulls back. The SEAS5 point numbers lean mild. The raw share colder than normal is 49%, but it mixes EC46 for December with the SEAS5 cold bias of -0.67 °C. SEAS5 alone against its own climate gives 24%, or 20 to 27% after we round the values. The same SEAS5 members against the ERA5 normal give 53%. I weight the bias-corrected 24% most, because none of the three is calibrated on past skill.

EC46 makes December 4.5 °C against the 4.1 °C normal, with 67% of members warmer. The February NAO signal disagrees with the fast vortex rebuild for January, so I keep January mild and hold the cold tilt for February. Where the maps show mild and the stratosphere shows a block, I weight the stratosphere for late November and December. I weight the strong seasonal NAO above its size, because seasonal models understate the NAO. I weight the stratosphere and the drivers above the analogs, which carry no skill here.

The QBO is westerly, +15.9 m/s at 30 hPa and +13.5 m/s at 50 hPa in October. It favours a fast rebuild and fewer mid-winter disruptions, so it lowers the cold odds. The MJO is weak, phase 4 at amplitude 1.31 on 11 November. ECMWF ENS takes it to phase 4 near the circle by day 5, then inside it. GEFS keeps it near phases 3 and 4 and mostly inside the circle to 28 November. So neither reaches phases 6 and 7, and neither pushes a negative NAO.

The North Sea is +0.77 °C against 1991-2020, with 36% of cells above +1 °C. It gives heavy showers in an easterly but keeps snow at the coast marginal. The tripole is -0.61, a weak positive-NAO pattern. The Barents and Kara Seas are +1.73 °C in open water, linked to a weaker vortex. Eurasian snow is 14.55 million km2, below the 16.06 normal and rank 41 of 61, so not the cold-signal pattern.

Upwind, Oslo has snow on the ground in 55 to 76% of members after 16 November, but Stockholm and Helsinki have almost none. Cold air aloft builds to the north-east late in the month. On 26 November, 39% of members reach -8 °C at 850 hPa over Helsinki and 31% over Oslo. Copenhagen, the nearest point on the easterly track, reaches it in only 12%. So an easterly from this track stays marginal for snow.

Judah Cohen's blog of 9 November expects a stretched vortex, cold in East Asia and North America, and a short positive AO. I agree on the stretch and on the positive AO blip, which GEFS shows near +1.0 on 20 November. I differ on two points. The 10 hPa wind reversed, so this is a major warming under the scored rule. And ECMWF ENS takes the 500 hPa cap to +1 sd in 59% of members, so the troposphere answers.

The Met Office text for 20 to 29 November has a changeable Atlantic pattern with some snow in the north, and I agree. For 30 November to 14 December it tracks lows south of normal, with a drier, colder north, and I agree on the block. But the ECMWF maps keep the UK at 0 to +1 °C with the low to the west. So I give snow and ice in early December less weight than the text does.

The analog set is outside the record, with no measurable skill, so I give it no weight. The nearest winters on El Nino and the QBO alone average +0.2 °C, within chance. The 4 winters with a major warming by 31 December average -0.3 °C, also within chance. No winter in the record had a November warming, so there is no true precedent. In Central England, a cold November leads to a cold winter 38% of the time, against 33% for all winters.

So I set a cold December to February at 30%, a medium chance. The deep warming, the block to mid-December and the February NAO signal lift it. El Nino, the westerly QBO, the fast mid-December rebuild and the mild EC46 December hold it down. I put it above the SEAS5 own-climate 24%, because that issue predates the warming. I put it below the raw shares near 49 to 53%, because they carry the model cold bias.

I set the cold spell at 48%, medium. The week to 22 November is cold, but a showery north-westerly seldom gives 5 nights at -3 °C in a row. The block from late November and the February easterly risk give later chances. I set the wet winter at 47%, lifted by the seasonal low near the UK, the warm North Sea and the warm western Atlantic. I set the stormy winter at 44%, because a negative NAO moves the jet south, but past cold winters had few stormy days. These are not a mirror of the cold odds, because a winter can be wet, stormy and cold at once.

For the warming months, November is 100%, because the event started on 10 November and the wind recovers well. December is 3%. A new event cannot start before about 3 December, after 20 westerly days, and no short-range member reverses to 30 November. January is 18%, below the 22% reference, because the westerly QBO and the fast rebuild pull it down. February is 22%, at the reference, because the El Nino tilt and the westerly QBO cancel.

My last outlook gave 30% cold, 48% for a spell, 47% wet and 44% stormy, and warming odds of 100%, 3%, 18% and 22%. This run uses a newer ECMWF run of 15 November and the 16 November stratosphere data, and it confirms the same picture. So my odds hold without change. Any change came from the weather, not from a new weight: the data now confirm the event and the fast recovery.

Its colder signs stand as follows. The 500 hPa sign of 50% or more of members at +1 sd on 25 to 30 November happened, at 55 to 59%. But the observed AO is not yet below -1, at -0.87 on 14 November and +0.06 on 15 November. The Scandinavian block sits 7 to 12 December with the low to the west, not south of Scotland, so that sign is not met. I cannot yet judge the Copenhagen -8 °C sign, because the data end on 28 November, and at most 12% reach it so far. A heat-flux pulse of 29 to 38 K m/s comes on 21 to 23 November in the forecast, not yet in the analysis.

No EC46 member turns easterly at 10 hPa in late December or January. The December seasonal issues are not out, near 5 December. The C3S February sign needs 6 of 8 centres with the low south of Scotland, not yet judged.

Its milder signs stand as follows. Most members no longer stay below +1 sd at 500 hPa on 25 to 30 November, because 59% reached it. NAO+ is not most likely on most days of 1 to 15 December. The 10 hPa wind stays near 38 m/s by mid-December, below the 45 m/s sign, but the pole is cold. The December weeks sit at 0 to +0.5 °C, so the every-week-above sign is not clearly met.

Only the 500 hPa coupling sign can no longer happen, and it resolved on the colder side. The December seasonal issue is not out. My odds hold because the weather did not move since the last run.
cold_windows: 16-22 November (high): a cold north-westerly to northerly behind a trough near the North Sea. The ECMWF meteogram keeps the week about 2 °C below normal. The city gets showers of rain, hail and sleet, with frost on clear nights. The Pentlands get snow showers and a thin cover on the tops. Five nights at -3 °C in a row stay unlikely in a showery wind.

22 November to 12 December (medium): a blocking high over Scandinavia, first with a low west of Ireland. The wind is south-easterly from a mild continent, so the city stays near normal, with fog, frost and cold rain on fronts. The Pentlands and Moorfoots get battleground snow if fronts stall against the block. A true easterly with snow showers needs the low south of Scotland and -8 °C air over Denmark, which only 12% of members show.

February (low): an easterly on the north side of a low over the UK and western Europe. Seven of eight seasonal centres show a strong Arctic high, and the SEAS5 NAO median is near -2.9. But SEAS5 alone keeps 65% of members warmer than its own February climate. The warm North Sea needs air aloft near -8 °C for snow at the coast. The city gets snow that lies a day or two at best, and the Pentlands get lying snow for days.

17-31 December (low): a ridge near the UK with a trough over Scandinavia, or a second vortex disruption. The EC46 500 hPa map for 21 to 28 December has this shape, but NAO+ is most likely on 13 to 21 December. One or two EC46 members reach 0 m/s at 10 hPa near late December. The city gets frost under the ridge and cold showers if the wind turns north, and the hills get snow showers.

March (low): late frost and short snowfalls in northerly or easterly outbreaks. The SEAS5 NAO median is near -2.4, and the point data give 8 frost days against 5.7. The city gets frost and brief snow, and the hills get lying snow after each outbreak.

January (low): mostly westerly or north-westerly flow behind a vortex that rebuilds to about 38 m/s. Four centres put a low near the UK, wet and near normal, and NCEP and Meteo-France put it over Scandinavia. The city gets rain, sleet in showers and frost on clear nights. Snow to low levels needs a block, and the warming chance is 18%.

snow_checklist: ✅ Polar vortex weakens or breaks down: the 60°N wind at 10 hPa reversed around 10 to 12 November, a record-early major warming. NASA GEOS shows -2.9 m/s on 11 November. It is westerly again near 5 m/s on 16 November and rebuilds to 24 to 36 m/s by 28 November.

🟡 AO and NAO negative for 2 weeks or more: both were negative from 9 November, and the NAO is -1.0 on 15 November. The AO rose to +0.06 on 15 November, then GEFS takes it to -1.8 by 30 November, with 84% of members negative.

🟡 Blocking high over Scandinavia or Greenland: no block sits there in the analysis yet. The ECMWF maps put +10 to +20 hPa over Scandinavia in the week from 23 November. The regimes make Scandinavian blocking most likely on 22 to 27 November.

🟡 Cold air in place upwind: Oslo has snow, but Stockholm and Helsinki have almost none, and Eurasian snow ranks 41 of 61. At 850 hPa, 39% of members reach -8 °C over Helsinki and 31% over Oslo on 26 November.

⬜ Cold enough aloft, about -8 °C at 850 hPa: Copenhagen is the nearest point on the easterly track. It reaches -8 °C in at most 12% of members to 28 November. The North Sea at +0.77 °C needs colder air than usual for coast snow.
⬜ It happens more than once, or lasts: no spell meets the rule yet, with 0 days to 10 November. The chances are the cold week to 22 November, the block from late November and the February risk.
❌ El Nino's grip loosens: the ONI is +2.46, the MEI v2 +2.53, a record, and the PNA +1.6. SEAS5 keeps Nino 3.4 near +4.0 °C in December and January and near +3.7 °C in February.

months.notes: The warming started on 10 November, and the AO fell to -1.98 on 12 November. The meteogram keeps 16 to 22 November about 2 °C below normal. A Scandinavian block follows from 22 November, with the low to the west, near +0.5 °C. The snow risk is mostly on the Pentlands, with sleet showers in the city.

ECMWF regimes make Scandinavian blocking most likely on 7 to 12 December and NAO+ on 13 to 21 December. The weekly maps keep the UK at 0 to +1 °C, with the low to the west. EC46 gives 4.5 °C against the 4.1 °C normal, with 67% of members warmer, and 87 mm against 77 mm. Fronts that stall against the block give battleground snow on the hills.

Four centres put a low near the UK, and NCEP and Meteo-France put it over Scandinavia. SEAS5 alone keeps 76% of members warmer than its own January climate. The point data give 4.0 °C against 3.9 °C and 74 mm against 74 mm. The warming chance is 18%, and the normal is 4.7 snow days.

Seven of eight centres show a strongly negative NAO, and the SEAS5 median is near -2.9. Most put the low over the UK or western Europe, so Scotland sits near its north edge, an easterly risk. But SEAS5 alone keeps 65% of members warmer than its own February climate. The point data give 3.8 °C against 4.1 °C and 69 mm against 62 mm.

The SEAS5 NAO median is near -2.4, and GloSea keeps an Arctic high with lower pressure over Europe. SEAS5 alone keeps 75% of members warmer than its own March climate. The point data give 5.0 °C against 5.3 °C, with 8 frost days against 5.7. A late block can bring frost and short snowfalls.

drivers: Polar vortex: a major sudden stratospheric warming started on 10 November. NASA GEOS shows -2.9 m/s at 60°N and 10 hPa on 11 November, a record low for the date. The 10 hPa wind is near 5 m/s on 16 November, below the weakest value for the date in the ERA5 record. This is the earliest major warming in the record, on NASA MERRA-2 since 1979/80.

Depth: the two measures disagree. The 50 hPa wind stays westerly at 7 to 12 m/s, near the 10th percentile. The 100 hPa cap reached +2.19 sd on 4 November. It returns above +1 sd in 61% of ECMWF ENS, 88% of AIFS ENS and 52% of GEPS members, but 0% of GEFS. So the event is deep.

Surface answer: ECMWF ENS takes the 500 hPa cap to +1 sd in half of its members from 25 November, and 59% on 26 November. But the low sits west of Ireland and the high over Scandinavia, so Edinburgh gets a south-easterly near normal, not deep cold.

Shape: the ECMWF ENS mean puts the vortex off the pole towards Scandinavia on 19 November. It stretches the vortex from Canada to Siberia on 24 November. The wave-2 ridges tilt west with height, but the 10 hPa wind rises, so this is a stretch, not a split.

Wave forcing: the 100 hPa heat flux peaked at 46.4 K m/s on 29 October, mostly in wave 2. A second pulse of 29 to 38 K m/s comes on 21 to 23 November. It meets a vortex that rebuilds, so it reverses the vortex in no member.

Pacific chain: the mountain torque over East Asia reached +4.0 sd on 8 November, and angular momentum rose from +0.3 sd to +2.8 sd by 15 November. The PNA is +1.6, and ECMWF ENS puts 61% of members at an EPO of -1 or below on 21 November. The chain follows in part.

El Nino: very strong and east Pacific, with the ONI at +2.46, the RONI at +1.97 and a record MEI v2 of +2.53. The nearest same weeks are 1997 by flavour and 2015 by Nino 3.4. The class leans mild here and in Central England, mostly within chance.
QBO: westerly, +15.9 m/s at 30 hPa and +13.5 m/s at 50 hPa in October. It favours a fast rebuild and fewer mid-winter disruptions, so it lowers the cold odds.
MJO: weak, phase 4 at amplitude 1.31 on 11 November. ECMWF ENS and GEFS keep it near phases 3 and 4 and mostly inside the circle, so neither pushes a negative NAO.
Angular momentum: +2.8 sd on 15 November, with the Global Wind Oscillation in phase 6 at 2.95, the El Nino state with an extended Pacific jet.
Sea temperatures: the North Sea is +0.77 °C, so coast snow stays marginal. The tripole is -0.61, a weak positive-NAO sign. The Barents and Kara Seas are +1.73 °C, linked to a weaker vortex.

Snow and cold upwind: Eurasian snow is 14.55 million km2, rank 41 of 61, below the 16.06 normal. Oslo has snow, Stockholm and Helsinki do not, and Copenhagen reaches -8 °C at 850 hPa in at most 12% of members.

Extended range: the ECMWF regimes give Scandinavian blocking on 22 to 27 November and 7 to 12 December, and NAO+ on 13 to 21 December. EC46 keeps Arctic pressure near +0.4 sd in late November, then near 0.

Seasonal models: the November issue predates the warming. It puts the UK at 0 to +1 °C, but seven of eight centres show a strongly negative NAO in February. I weight the NAO signal up and the mild maps down.
Analogs: outside the record, with no measurable skill, so they get no weight. The nearest El Nino and QBO winters average +0.2 °C, and the 4 winters with an early warming -0.3 °C, both within chance.

Model verification for Edinburgh: forecasts made 1/3/5/7 days ahead vs ERA5 reanalysis, last 40 days (temp_mae in °C, lower is better; wet_dry_hit_pct = share of days the model got right whether it would rain over 1 mm). 'Claude (this page)' is your own previous forecasts, scored the same way (its rain call counts a chance of 50% or more, or medium or high risk, as rain); use its biases to correct yourself. 'reliability' scores your own rain chances (Brier, 0 is perfect) against ECMWF ENS on the same days and against the window's wet-day share, and your weekly tilts for the extended-range weeks against ERA5's weekly mean. 'station' is the same check against EGPH's own observed daily highs and lows (METAR; complete the next day, so it includes the last week that ERA5 hasn't reached; half-hourly integer readings, so its highs run a few tenths low). station.tmin_by_night is the airport-trained correction of the models' lows by type of night (per lead: each model's all-night bias, and per class the nights, the mean model bias on such a night (bias) and the part the blend removes after shrinkage (used_bias)); recent_1day the last nights one day ahead; blend_by_night the blend's own logged lows scored at the airport by the type of night it forecast, out of sample

items.title: ECMWF seasonal ensemble by month for Edinburgh vs ERA5 1991-2020 normals. This is Open-Meteo's default seasonal series: EC46 (run daily) for about the first 46 days, then SEAS5 (started on the 1st of each month), 51 members joined by member number, on a 36 km grid, so the first month or two are mostly EC46. Raw model output, not bias-corrected: the model's own climate at this point differs from ERA5's normal by month and lead (the SEAS5 winter call's model_climate.by_month gives bias_c, and pct_members_warmer_than_model_climate for SEAS5 alone against its own climate), so pct_members_warmer_than_normal here mixes the forecast with that bias. Compare the spread and the shares, not the absolute values

ECMWF's own implied calls on the cold-winter event, from the point members. pct_members_colder_than_normal (logged beside your call and scored as the rival 'ECMWF SEAS5') is the share of the 51 members of the default series above (EC46 for about 46 days, then SEAS5, joined by member number, so its December is mostly EC46) with a December-February mean of (daily max + min) / 2 below the ERA5 1991-2020 normal. It is raw model output, so it mixes the forecast with the model's own error at this point, and it is against ERA5, not the ERA5-Land the odds are scored on. pct_members_colder_than_model_climate is SEAS5 alone (model_climate.run_start is the first month of the reply; in the first days of a month the newest run can still be the month before): the share of its members whose December-February mean is below SEAS5's own climate for the same start month and lead (ECMWF's monthly anomaly, from its re-forecasts; model_climate.climate says which years). That removes the model's mean error at this point (model_climate.by_month gives it month by month as bias_c, the model climate minus the ERA5 normal) but not errors in the spread, and it is not calibrated on the model's past skill. model_climate.djf.pct_range_for_rounding is how far the 0.1 °C rounding of ECMWF's figures can move it; pct_same_members_colder_than_era5_normal is the same SEAS5 members against the ERA5 normal without the correction, so the three shares separate the EC46 part from the bias part. None of them is the answer: they are inputs to weigh

model_climate.note: The model climate is the mean of the past forecasts that SEAS5 makes for the same start month and the same lead. A share below this climate removes the mean error of the model at this point. It does not correct the spread of the members, the change in climate between the two periods, or the difference between ERA5 and ERA5-Land.

items.title: Polar vortex strength: zonal-mean zonal wind at 60°N (m/s, daily UTC mean, positive = westerly) at 10 hPa (the standard SSW level: a reversal to easterly is a major sudden stratospheric warming) and 50 hPa (lower stratosphere), per model; ensembles give mean/p10/p90/min across members and the % of members easterly. Early-warning signs from the single runs: polar_cap_t10 = area-mean temperature over 60-90°N at 10 hPa (°C; a jump of 20 °C or more in a few days is a sudden warming under way), heat_flux_100 = eddy heat flux v'T' around 60°N at 100 hPa (K m/s; sustained high values push wave energy up and tend to weaken the vortex 1-2 weeks later; w1 and w2 are the parts of it carried by zonal wavenumbers 1 and 2: a pulse mostly in wave 1 tends to displace the vortex, one with a large wave-2 part to stretch and split it), waves_10hPa = amplitude in metres of zonal wavenumber 1 and 2 in the 10 hPa geopotential height around 60°N (wave 1 growing to well over 1000 m means the vortex is being displaced off the pole; wave 2 growing to several hundred metres means it is being stretched towards a split; in winter a few hundred metres each is ordinary; waves_vs_season places today against this season's analysed days). wave2_by_level gives, per single run and day, the longitude (°E, 0-180; the second ridge is 180° further east) of the wave-2 ridges in the 60°N height at 500, 100 and 10 hPa, their amplitudes, and the tilt (10 hPa ridge minus 500 hPa ridge): a ridge that shifts west with height (negative tilt, e.g. 45°E at 500, 29°E at 100, 6°E at 10 hPa) with ridges near the Urals and Alaska is the structure of a split. For ensembles, pct_members_ever_easterly is the share of members that reverse on any day of the run (the SSW probability for that window; the per-day share understates it) and reversal_median_date the typical timing. Days before 2026-11-21 are analysis.

Negative = a ridge over Alaska: Arctic air into North America, and often more upward wave flux into the stratosphere a week or two later, so read it beside the 100 hPa heat flux. Positive = a trough near Alaska and mild Pacific air. Ensembles give the mean, the 5th/25th/75th/95th percentiles and the share of members at -1 or below each day; single runs start 5 days back. Days before 2026-11-21 are analysis. It can differ a little from other sites' EPO, which use other climatologies and grids

periods.text: The UK is likely to remain in some degree of 'battleground' scenario through much of this period, as Atlantic weather systems butt up against high pressure to the east or northeast of the UK. As such, western and southwestern areas are most likely to be wettest, whereas drier conditions are more probable towards the north and east. That said, some precipitation is possible for all parts at times. There remains the potential for snow, especially across the higher ground of northern UK. In the north, temperatures overall could be below normal during this period and perhaps closer to normal in the south, and the boundary between milder/colder conditions will be determined by how far Atlantic fronts push across the UK.

The track of low pressure systems will likely be further south than normal during this period. This means that rainfall will probably be focused across the south of the UK with a risk of stronger winds at times; conversely, higher pressure developing to the north means drier and more settled conditions are more likely here. Temperatures in the south will probably be near normal or perhaps slightly above at times, with the north colder than normal, although either bias could extended to cover a wider area of the UK.
